text.p: Swedish drugs company Astra on Monday depressed the market with a lower-than-expected profit for the first three months of 1997, blamed largely on stockpiling prior to the end of 1996.
Astra's share price tumbled 22 crowns ($2.88) to 320.5 crowns after the company reported pre-tax profits rose just one percent to 3.46 billion crowns against expections of 3.93 billion crowns.
Sales in the three months ending March 31 rose nine percent to 10.13 billion crowns -- but operating earnings only rose six percent to 3.36 billion crowns.

"Inventory building in the fourth quarter of 1996 had been under-appreciated by the whole market and led to an overshot in sales by about 400-500 million crowns," analyst Stuart Harris from Dresdner Kleinwort Benson told Reuters.
"The company needs to do a good job at the analysts' meeting (Tuesday) when it will face a barrage of questions."
Analysts said the report had left a realm of questions unanswered -- and could lead to some analysts' downgrading their forecasts for Astra's annual earnings.
Financial items fell to 92 million crowns from 257 million.
Research and development costs rose 23 percent to 1.88 billion crowns.
"The result was disappointing and surprising," said analyst Marie Helene Leopold from Paribas. "It's left everyone a bit perplexed."
However some analysts said the reaction was overdone.
"Astra's report was really not so bad as to deserve this market reaction," said Aros analyst Ingemar Kihlstrom.
"In the long term Astra is a good buy."
Sales of all of Astra's key products continued to grow.
Astra's sales of blockbuster anti-ulcer drug Losec, sold as Prilosec in the U.S., rose 14 percent to 4.80 billion crowns while total world sales of Losec rose to 7.05 billion crowns from 5.9 billion.
Sales of Astra's second biggest drug, the anti-asthma agent Pulmicort, rose nine percent to 1.21 billion crowns.
Its third main product, beta-blocker Seloken, Astra's largest product in the cardiovascular area, gained four percent to 638 million crowns.
"Sales development during the first quarter of 1997 was affected by a certain amount of patient and wholesaler stockpiling prior to year-end 1996, especially in Sweden," Astra said in a statement.
"The above-mentioned stockpiling also impacted earnings."
Astra spokesman Staffan Ternby did not say how great an impact the stockpiling had on earnings.
"It had an effect of about 400 million crowns on sales," he said, adding that sales were unusually high last November and December.
"But the fundamental underlying factors are still positive," he told Reuters.
However he said the market had developed in a worse manner than expected but it was hard to know if this would continue.
"It is hard to know but there is nothing fundamentally that backs this up. There is no crisis or anything," he said. ($ = 7.625 Swedish Crowns)
